Her work is represented in major collections including the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm, the Victoria and Albert Museum in London and the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam.

products.name: Vase 'Tulip' designed by Nils Landberg for Orrefors
products.description: This tall Tulip vase was designed by Nils Landberg for Orrefors in Sweden in 1957 and rises 44.5 cm in height. Landberg was one of the foremost designers at Orrefors, and his Tulip series is celebrated for its slender, elongated silhouette and demanding execution in mouth-blown glass. The vase embodies the refined, nature-attuned elegance that made Orrefors a flagship of Swedish glass during the mid twentieth century.

products.name: Vase 'Ventana' designed by Mona Morales-Schildt for Kosta
products.description: This vase belongs to the Ventana series created by Mona Morales-Schildt for Kosta, a series begun in 1959 and produced through the following decade. Morales-Schildt joined Kosta in 1958, and the series name, meaning window in Spanish, points to the window-like planes of colour for which these layered glass vases are known. Compact and signed, the vase is a refined example of her lyrical contribution to Swedish glass.

products.name: A set of 27 piece tableware 'Pencil' designed by Stig Lindberg for Gustavsberg
products.description: This 27-piece tableware set comes from the 'Pencil' series by Stig Lindberg for Gustavsberg and reflects the restrained elegance of post-war Scandinavian table design. Executed in fine bone china, it is decorated with delicate black linear motifs that resemble quick pencil strokes drawn across the white surface. The set consists of eleven dinner plates, twelve starter plates and four bowls, combining everyday practicality with Lindberg's highly individual graphic language. It remains one of the clearest examples of the Swedish ideal of creating beautiful objects for ordinary life.

products.name: Bowl designed by Rolf Palm
products.description: This ceramic bowl by Swedish studio potter Rolf Palm exemplifies the refined artistry of Scandinavian ceramic design in the mid-20th century. Hand-thrown and signed by the artist, it displays Palm's signature earthy glaze palette of muted tones, speckled surfaces and subtle variations that highlight the handmade process. The softly rounded form and tactile finish reflect his mastery of traditional stoneware techniques, developed over decades at his studio in Mölle, Sweden. The piece bridges functionality and sculpture with a distinctly Nordic sensibility.

products.name: Bowl designed by Stig Lindberg, Gustavsberg
products.description: An asymmetrical boat-shaped bowl designed by Stig Lindberg for Gustavsberg in Sweden during the 1940s and 1950s. It is executed in faience with a smooth, glossy white glaze, and the interior is painted with stylized leaves in chartreuse, golden yellow, teal and brown. The graceful upturned form and lively hand-painted decoration capture the playful graphic language that made Lindberg one of Sweden's most influential ceramicists of the twentieth century.

products.name: Bowl designed by Vicke Lindstrand for Upsala Ekeby
products.description: This bowl designed by Vicke Lindstrand for Upsala Ekeby showcases his unique approach to form and decoration, seamlessly blending figuration with expressive painterly techniques. The earthenware body carries hand-painted stylized figures in the modernist spirit Lindstrand brought to Swedish pottery after joining Upsala-Ekeby in 1942. Having earlier pioneered Graal glass at Orrefors, he transferred the same graphic confidence to ceramics, as this piece beautifully demonstrates.

products.name: Bowl 'Farsta' designed by Wilhelm Kåge for Gustavsberg, Sweden, 1959
products.description: A bowl from the celebrated Farsta series by Wilhelm Kåge, produced at the Gustavsberg studio in Sweden in 1959. The Farsta series, made between 1930 and 1960, is among Kåge's most exclusive work, prized for its richly mottled stoneware glazes. The bowl's organic form and layered, flowing glaze make every example unique, exemplifying the studio's pursuit of ceramic art at its highest level.

products.name: Dragon sculpture designed by Wilhelm Kåge for Gustavsberg
products.description: Wilhelm Kåge's dragon sculptures, crafted at Gustavsberg from the late 1930s to the 1950s, exemplify his innovative approach to ceramic art. This stoneware example shows the stylized forms typical of the series, with pronounced eyes, a curled tail and a richly textured body. Affectionately known as drakvalpar, or dragon puppies, these creatures offered Kåge expressive freedom and a blend of humour and fantasy that contrasted with the restrained aesthetics of his tableware. The sculpture showcases a mix of whimsical design and Kåge's exceptional craftsmanship.

products.name: Mandrill sculpture designed by Vicke Lindstrand for Uppsala Ekeby, Sweden, 1940s
products.description: A stoneware sculpture of a mandrill designed by Vicke Lindstrand for Uppsala Ekeby in Sweden during the 1940s. The figure captures the animal's powerful frame and expressive features with a sculptor's eye for character and movement. Lindstrand was one of Sweden's most influential designers of the twentieth century, and his ceramic animal figures from this period combine simplified modern forms with lively, hand-finished surfaces.

products.name: Ceramic planter designed by Margareta Wibom for Bo Fajans
products.description: This ceramic planter by Margareta (Maggie) Wibom is defined by its sculptural relief of stylised vines and leaves wrapping rhythmically around the body. Executed in chamotted stoneware, it combines robust construction with expressive surface treatment, reflecting the transition from Swedish Grace to early modernism. Produced by Bo Fajans in Gävle during the interwar years, it testifies to the factory's reputation for high-quality artistic ceramics. Wibom was among the first women to establish herself in Swedish ceramic design, and her relief work is rooted in both tradition and modern expression.

products.name: Plate designed by Tyra Lundgren for Rörstrand
products.description: This elegant stoneware dish designed by Tyra Lundgren for Rörstrand is a distinguished example of early Nordic mid-century design in ceramics. Executed in high-fired stoneware, the surface carries a softly modulated blue underglaze and features a motif of a woman integrated into the form. The impressed Rörstrand signature with date underlines the dish's authentic place in the factory's artistic production of the period. Lundgren worked as a designer at Rörstrand during the late 1920s and early 1930s, when the factory was exploring more sculptural and modern approaches, and this example is signed TL Rörstrand 1930.

products.name: Plate designed by Tyra Lundgren for Rörstrand, Sweden, 1930s
products.description: A hand-painted ceramic plate designed by Tyra Lundgren for Rörstrand in Sweden during the 1930s. The cream-ground surface is decorated in cobalt blue with a seated female figure shown in profile, holding a fan, her drapery rendered in bold, expressive brushwork. Lundgren, who worked at Rörstrand in the late 1920s and early 1930s, was one of the most versatile Swedish artists of her generation, moving fluently between ceramics, glass and painting. This plate exemplifies the painterly, figurative direction of the factory's artistic faience during the period.

products.name: Alligator sculpture retailed by Svenskt Tenn, Italy, 1950s
products.description: This hand-modelled terracotta sculpture depicts an alligator rendered in naturalistic form, modelled fully in the round with individually shaped scales, limbs and tail. It is finished with a glossy green-brown glaze, and the irregularities in the modelling indicate studio or workshop production rather than moulded manufacture. The piece was made in Italy during the 1950s and retailed by Svenskt Tenn in Stockholm, a firm known for its curated selection of handcrafted decorative pieces. Animal sculptures in ceramic formed a recurring category in Svenskt Tenn's mid-century assortment, valued for their tactile qualities and sculptural presence.

products.name: Sculpture, Italy, 1950s
products.description: A charming ceramic figure of a seated basset hound made in Italy during the 1950s. The dog is modelled in a realistic sitting pose with long drooping ears and finely textured, wrinkled skin, finished in a glossy glaze of warm orange-brown and creamy white. Anonymous workshop production of this period often achieved great character, and this sculpture combines decorative appeal with lifelike detail.

products.name: Monkey sculpture attributed to Gunnar Nylund, 20th Century
products.description: A stoneware sculpture of a seated monkey, attributed to Gunnar Nylund. The figure rests in a contemplative pose with one hand raised to its head, rendered with expressive facial features and stylized musculature. It is finished in a two-tone glaze with a creamy tan body contrasted by dark brown on the face, hands and feet. Nylund was artistic director at Rörstrand and one of the leading Scandinavian ceramicists of the twentieth century.

products.name: Sculpture by Hassan Heshmat
products.description: A unique, signed ceramic sculpture by Hassan Heshmat depicting a seated mother tenderly embracing her child. The flowing, stylized figures with serene, closed-eyed expressions are finished in a variegated glaze blending cerulean blue, turquoise and pale green with subtle brown undertones. Heshmat's hand-built work combines humanist subject matter with a soft, sculptural treatment of the clay.

products.name: Sculpture by Tyra Lundgren for Rörstrand, Sweden, 1930
products.description: A faience sculpture by Tyra Lundgren for Rörstrand, Sweden, dated 1930. It depicts a figure in a dynamic crouched pose riding a large fish, the base glazed in vibrant turquoise and pale yellow-green with textured scale patterns. The smooth, glossy white figure and fluid, organic forms give the piece a distinctly Art Deco character. Lundgren was among the most versatile Swedish artists of the twentieth century, working across ceramics, glass and painting.

products.name: Sculpture 'Springare' designed by Stig Lindberg for Gustavsberg
products.description: The 'Springare' by Stig Lindberg is a refined ceramic sculpture from Sweden's mid-20th-century design era, crafted in the 1950s for the Gustavsberg porcelain factory. It interprets the theme of a horse in sculptural form, its softly rounded body, spindly legs and minimal head embodying Lindberg's characteristic blend of humour, elegance and craft. This version features a light stoneware glaze with subtle painted and incised detailing, offering both visual calm and textural interest.

products.name: Three zebras by Vicke Lindstrand for Upsala Ekeby, Sweden, 1940s
products.description: A stoneware sculpture group of three zebras designed by Vicke Lindstrand for Upsala Ekeby, Sweden, during the 1940s. The figures are modelled with lively, simplified forms and painted striping that gives the group its strong graphic appeal. Lindstrand introduced a modernist sensibility to Swedish ceramics after joining Upsala-Ekeby in 1942, and animal groups such as this are among his most sought-after works.

products.name: Vase designed by Hans Vangsø
products.description: This vase designed by Danish potter Hans Vangsø has a thick white glaze and a heavily textured surface, with cratered openings, small dark inclusions and areas where the glaze has fused with the clay body, giving the piece a distinctly geological character. Vangsø pours his glazes thickly and uses unconventional combustible materials such as seaweed, salt, metals and newspaper during the firing process. The compact, rounded form recalls East Asian ceramic traditions, particularly moon jars, while the treatment remains closely tied to Danish studio pottery. The vase is monogrammed with Vangsø's signature mark.

products.name: Vase designed by Liisa Hallamaa for Arabia
products.description: A stoneware vase designed by Liisa Hallamaa for the Finnish manufacturer Arabia in the 1950s. The vase pairs a simple, modern vessel form with the richly glazed surface typical of Arabia's art ceramics of the period. Hallamaa was among the Finnish ceramicists who brought colour and sculptural presence to post-war domestic design.

products.name: Vase designed by Mette Doller for Alfred Johansson
products.description: A stoneware vase designed by Mette Doller for Alfred Johansson in Sweden during the 1950s. Doller was known for her precise, modern approach to ceramics, and the vase's clean proportions reflect the restrained elegance of Swedish design in the period. The Alfred Johansson workshop supplied the high-quality stoneware that gave designers like Doller an ideal canvas for their forms.

products.name: Vase model 352 designed by Vicke Lindstrand
products.description: A glazed ceramic vase, model 352, designed by Vicke Lindstrand in Sweden in 1944–48. The vase combines a sculptural modern profile with a rich glaze, characteristic of Lindstrand's ceramic work of the mid-1940s. Lindstrand was one of Sweden's most influential twentieth-century designers, moving between pioneering glass at Orrefors and expressive ceramics at Upsala-Ekeby.

products.name: Vase 'Model 385' designed by Vicke Lindstrand for Uppsala Ekeby
products.description: This glazed earthenware vase was designed by Vicke Lindstrand for Uppsala-Ekeby and is decorated in light yellow and brown glazes with incised female figures set against a mottled ceramic surface. The sgraffito technique, in which the contours of the figures are incised directly into the clay body before firing, gives the line work a physical presence within the surface rather than appearing only as painted decoration. The vase is signed 'Vicke' at the base and stamped 'Ekeby 385 V.L' underneath. Lindstrand's ceramics from this period often combine hand-drawn decoration with simplified forms, frequently depicting figures, animals and mythological subjects.

products.name: Vase/candlestick 'Snurran' by Stig Lindberg for Gustavsberg
products.description: Stig Lindberg's 'Snurran' belongs to a limited and timeless series for Gustavsberg whose name refers to the vessel's ability to be turned. Depending on its orientation, the piece functions as two vases with a central candle holder, or alternatively as two candle holders with a single vase. Executed in stoneware and signed with Studiohånden, it captures the whimsical, playful and optimistic spirit of Lindberg's post-war work. Lindberg was appointed artistic director at Gustavsberg in 1949 and brought a strong graphic sensibility to Swedish ceramics.

products.name: Wall hanging sculpture by Tyra Lundgren, Sweden, 1927
products.description: A stoneware wall-hanging sculpture by Tyra Lundgren, made in Sweden in 1927. The relief is modelled with the sculptural confidence Lundgren developed during her years at Rörstrand, combining figuration with a modern, decorative treatment of the surface. Lundgren was one of the most versatile Swedish artists of the twentieth century, and early wall works such as this are rare examples of her sculptural ceramics. A striking piece that brings Nordic Art Deco character to the interior.

products.name: Composition by Rune Hagberg
products.description: Rune Hagberg (1924 - 2015) was a self-taught pupil of Zen Buddhism who explored silence and introspection within his work. Born in Uppsala, Sweden, Hagberg became heavily influenced by Eastern calligraphy throughout his life – and developed a spontaneous sign painting style with a strong concentration on a select amount of characters rooted in Zen Buddhism. His informal meditative practice found its place between concretism and expressionism which was widespread in the 1950s. Later in his life, these symbols would be bound into reels and tied together with string - white, ascetic, and secretive within their frames. Eventually, Hagberg's practice came to focus on a gradual loosening of the picture surface, a kind of elimination of the sheet of paper, as if to approach the idea of nothingness. This exploration later found expression in sculptural objects. His oeuvre of ink painting turned him into a public figure in Sweden – hosting a long series of exhibitions, most notably at Moderna Museet in Malmö and Norrköping Art Museum. He also exhibited abroad in Japan in 1955 alongside a group of Eastern painters and calligraphers. Signed

products.name: Painting by Albert Johansson
products.description: This abstract painting by Albert Johansson, executed in oil on board during the 1960s, demonstrates the artist’s exploration of geometric form and spatial tension. Bold black shapes intersect with fields of red and white, while fine linear contours frame and guide the composition. A defining element of Johansson’s work is the use of lines that appear to “cut” across the surface of the painting. These directional lines divide the composition into shifting planes, producing a sense of expansion beyond the physical limits of the image. This approach aligns Johansson with the ideas of concrete art and reflects the influence of the Swedish artist Olle Baertling, whose exploration of infinite space through angular structures shaped much of the period’s abstract language. Albert Johansson (1926–1998) studied at Isaac Grünewald’s painting school before continuing his education at the Modern Art School in Stockholm. Although his earliest works were influenced by Surrealism, he soon moved toward a non-figurative mode of expression. Johansson later became known for his rigorous abstract compositions, where line, colour and geometry interact to create structured yet visually expansive works. Signed.

products.name: Painting by Bo Andersson
products.description: Mixed media on sheet metal by the Swedish artist Bo Andersson, executed in 1997. The composition is presented on a solid metal support and measures H 106 × W 66 cm, the mixed-media surface giving the work its layered, tactile character. Acquired directly from the artist in 1997, the piece carries the reference number 1941.

products.name: Painting by Mogens Andersen
products.description: Mogens Andersen’s works are masterful examples of contrast and colour play, varying wildly from image to image. His main interests lay in French Modernism, and he spent long periods in Paris until 1964; his friendships with Pierre Soulages and Jean Bazaine allowed him to develop his signature dark arabesques. After settling back in his home country of Denmark, he continued working until he lost all sight at 82. During his lengthy career, Andersen received the Eckersberg and Thorvaldsen medals, among various other honours. Signed.

products.name: Painting by Per-Erik Böklin
products.description: This gouache from 1955 is a finely balanced example of Per-Erik Böklin’s contribution to Swedish concrete art during the postwar period. The composition is constructed from interlocking geometric planes, where angled forms and curved elements generate a measured sense of movement across the surface. A restrained palette of cool blues, greens, and muted neutrals reinforces the architectural clarity of the design. Executed in gouache, the work benefits from the medium’s opacity and matte surface, allowing Böklin to define crisp edges and layered forms with precision. His use of gouache during the mid-1950s marked an important phase in his practice, later recognised in an exhibition at Galerie Bel'Art devoted specifically to these works. Per-Erik Böklin was a central figure within the Swedish concrete art movement and closely associated with the Ny realitet group. Trained as an engineer at Chalmers University of Technology, he approached painting with a structural mindset, viewing the artist as an active participant in shaping modern society alongside architects and engineers. Signed.

products.name: Painting by Sophie Tottie
products.description: This mixed-media painting by Sophie Tottie dates from the 1990s and exemplifies her exploratory approach to surface, material and abstraction. Built up through layers of paint and collage on a coarse textile ground, the composition balances intense fields of blue and black against the raw, fibrous texture of the support. Drips, ruptures, and irregular edges remain visible, allowing the physical process of making to play an active role in the finished work. Sophie Tottie, born in 1954, lives and works in Stockholm. She studied at the Royal Institute of Art in Stockholm and at the Institut des Hautes Études en Arts Plastiques in Paris, and has held professorial positions at several leading Swedish art institutions. Her work has been widely exhibited and is represented in major public and private collections, securing her position as one of the central figures in contemporary Swedish abstraction. Signed.

products.name: Painting by Sven Hansson
products.description: Working in a purely geometric, non-figurative style, Sven Hansson was a Swedish painter who is now represented in various municipalities in his home country, including the Museum of Modern Art. His gouache, oil, and relief pieces throughout the 1970’s to late 90’s are quietly expressive forms of contemporary art, on occasion using vibrant colour, many examples pure white and therefore reliant on natural light and the resulting shadows. Hansson pursued his artistic education at Valand's Art School in Gothenburg and further honed his skills under the mentorship of André Lhote at Académie André Lhote in Paris. André Lhote (1885–1962) was a prominent French painter, sculptor, and art teacher known for his significant contributions to Cubism and his role as an influential educator in modern art. Signed.

products.name: Painting by Sven Hansson

products.name: Painting 'Homage à Tatlin III' by Ole Schwalbe
products.description: This 1962 oil painting, titled ‘Homage à Tatlin III’, is an exceptional work by Danish modernist painter Ole Schwalbe. Paying tribute to Russian constructivist Vladimir Tatlin, Schwalbe explores geometric abstraction through bold shapes and striking colour fields. The canvas features a minimalist composition in varying shades of deep blue, accented by precise black lines and rounded forms, reflecting the influence of constructivist ideals. The painting is divided into distinct sections, with sharp rectangles and lines anchoring the composition on the left, contrasted by the curved shapes to the right. The careful balance of flat planes and subtle texture speaks to Schwalbe’s ability to harmonize opposing forces within his work, a hallmark of his geometric abstract style. Signed.

products.name: Painting 'Komposition I' by Ole Schwalbe
products.description: Komposition I from 1959 is a rigorous and concentrated work from Ole Schwalbe’s formative years within Danish Constructivism. Built from sharply defined rectangular fields, the composition balances black, white, and red in a tightly controlled arrangement. During the late 1950s, Schwalbe deliberately reduced his use of colour to these three tones. This limitation allowed Schwalbe to focus fully on relationships between form, colour, and spatial rhythm. Ole Schwalbe was a central figure in the second generation of Danish Constructivists, associated with the Linien group and the movement they termed concrete realism. Although trained as a lithographer, he was largely self-taught as a painter and approached painting as an autonomous visual system, free from representation. Signed

products.name: Painting 'No. II' by Harry Booström
products.description: Harry Booström’s abstract compositions from the 1950’s are a visual and geometric marvel, switching from abstract, to concretist and geometric shapes. His compositions achieve both dynamics and movement through this interplay of form and colour – this work would go on to be exhibited at various locations across Sweden, including the Artists of Söder Exhibition of 1955. Signed.

products.name: Painting 'Roman Days' by Ole Schwalbe
products.description: Roman Days , painted in 1964–65, is a clear and confident example of Ole Schwalbe’s mature abstract language. Composed of precisely drawn lines and geometric arcs set against a light ground, the work balances restraint with a renewed sensitivity to colour, marking a shift from the strict black-and-white palette that characterised much of his work during the 1950s. Schwalbe was a key figure in postwar Danish abstraction and a member of the Linien artists’ association, which helped define the second generation of Danish Constructivism, often referred to as concrete realism. A closely related nocturnal version of this composition, Romersk nat. Komposition (Roman Nights) , is held in the permanent collection of the National Gallery of Denmark, underscoring the significance of this body of work within Danish art history. Signed.

products.name: Painting 'Untitled' by Lennart Olausson
products.description: This mixed-media work by Lennart Olausson brings together soft, organic forms with a sharply constructed abstract framework. A large, coiling, almost cloud-like form occupies the centre of the composition, rendered in subtle shades of grey and black and set against blocks of deep crimson and black. The contrast between the cloud-like form and the rigid geometry surrounding it gives the work a dreamlike, slightly enigmatic quality, characteristic of Olausson’s interest in combining recognisable imagery with abstraction and ambiguity. Lennart Olausson made his gallery debut at Galleri Doktor Glas in Stockholm in 1968, followed by an exhibition at Galerie Belle in Västerås the following year. Educated at Konstfack and the Royal Institute of Art in Stockholm, Olausson developed a distinctive visual language combining precise observation, surreal elements and art-historical references. His work is represented in major Swedish collections including Moderna Museet and the Nationalmuseum. Signed Lennart Olausson

products.name: 'Untitled' by Rune Hagberg
products.material: Tempera on paper mounted on board
products.description: Rune Hagberg (1924 - 2015) was a self-taught pupil of Zen Buddhism who explored silence and introspection within his work. Born in Uppsala, Sweden, Hagberg became heavily influenced by Eastern calligraphy throughout his life – and developed a spontaneous sign painting style with a strong concentration on a select amount of characters rooted in Zen Buddhism. His informal meditative practice found its place between concretism and expressionism which was widespread in the 1950s. Later in his life, these symbols would be bound into reels and tied together with string - white, ascetic, and secretive within their frames. Eventually, Hagberg's practice came to focus on a gradual loosening of the picture surface, a kind of elimination of the sheet of paper, as if to approach the idea of nothingness. This exploration later found expression in sculptural objects. His oeuvre of ink painting turned him into a public figure in Sweden – hosting a long series of exhibitions, most notably at Moderna Museet in Malmö and Norrköping Art Museum. He also exhibited abroad in Japan in 1955 alongside a group of Eastern painters and calligraphers. Signed RH in pencil.

products.name: Bowl 'Il passagio - liten' or 'The passage - small' by Inger Sannes
products.description: This sculptural bowl titled Il passagio – liten (The Passage – small) was designed by Inger Sannes in 2014 and carved from white marble. The surface retains a distinctly tactile, almost geological quality, with rhythmically worked grooves that reveal both the resistance of the stone and the physical intensity of the carving process. Despite its weight and material density, the form appears open and poised, balancing mass with an unexpected sense of lightness. The work belongs to Sannes’ ongoing exploration of transition and transformation. A recurring idea in her practice is the dialogue between what is grounded and what is in motion: one element rooted and stable, the other pushing outward, suggesting growth, departure, or a shift in direction. Inger Sannes works between Stockholm and Pietrasanta, Italy, where she has access to the same marble traditions that shaped classical sculpture. Alongside her smaller works, she has realised major public commissions, including a large-scale version of Il Passaggio for Frösunda Kyrka in Gnesta, Sweden. Marked.

products.name: Framed sculpture 'Blåsegel' by Stig Åke Lund
products.description: This framed sculptural work, titled Blåsegel , was created in 1983 by the Swedish artist Stig Åke Lund. Constructed as a shallow relief, the piece combines layered elements into a compact, architectural composition that sits between sculpture and collage. Lund drew much of his visual language from nature, distilling organic motifs into simplified, botanical shapes. Throughout his career, Lund worked fluently across a wide range of media, including metal, wood, graphic techniques, and sculptural assemblage. His reliefs and montages often blur the boundary between image and object, inviting the viewer to read the work both as a composition and as a physical construction. Stig Åke Lund’s work is held in several important public collections, underscoring his international recognition. Institutions such as The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York and the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm include his works, situating Blåsegel within a broader body of refined Scandinavian mid century art.

products.name: Lizard sculpture

Formerly in the collection of Simon Spies, the piece unites mid-century decorative charm with genuine statement-piece character, holding its own in both classic and contemporary interiors.

products.name: Sculpture 'A fish called Matti'
products.description: Sculpture titled 'A fish called Matti', created by an anonymous Finnish artist in the 1980s. Measuring H 40 × W 120 × D 45 cm, the sculpture makes an eye-catching statement on a console or sideboard. A witty example of Nordic design humour, it brings character to both collector interiors and contemporary settings.

products.name: Sculpture 'Bull Terrier' by Sonja Petterson

products.name: Sculpture by Einar Höste
products.description: This sculptural work from the 1980s presents a delicately articulated structure built from interconnected geometric units, forming a continuous, net-like body that appears to expand freely across space. Constructed from repeated hexagonal and pentagonal frames, the sculpture recalls molecular or crystalline models, where each element is part of a larger, evolving system. The work reflects Höste's long-standing investigation into geometry as a means of understanding space. Throughout his practice, Höste explored the relationship between fundamental forms, most notably the cube and the sphere, and the tension between enclosed structure and open, expansive volume. Educated at Konstfack in Stockholm, Höste worked across sculpture and painting, often using industrial materials to construct abstract, space-defining works.

products.name: Sculpture by Hugo Liisberg
products.description: Hugo Liisberg (1896–1958) was a Danish sculptor and ceramicist celebrated for his dynamic depictions of the animal kingdom, where naturalistic observation meets dramatic tension. This bronze sculpture of an eagle striking a swan exemplifies his ability to capture the raw vitality of nature in motion. The raised wings and twisting bodies convey both elegance and struggle, a theme Liisberg often explored in his public commissions such as Ørnebrønden in Silkeborg 1931 and De vilde svaner in Odense 1951. Executed with a rich, green-brown patina, the work reveals Liisberg’s sculptural precision and sensitivity to surface texture, hallmarks of his practice that extended from monumental public works to smaller bronzes and ceramic figures produced for Royal Copenhagen and Saxbo. This piece reflects his enduring fascination with birds and the dramatic interplay between predator and prey, offering a powerful study of movement and form. Liisberg’s artistic significance is underscored by his presence in major museum collections, including Vejen Kunstmuseum, Museum Sønderjylland, Trapholt, Statens Museum for Kunst, KØS – Museum for kunst i det offentlige rum, ARoS Aarhus Kunstmuseum, and Esbjerg Kunstmuseum. Signed.

products.name: Sculpture by Lennart Färnmark
products.description: Large sculpture by the Swedish artist Lennart Färnmark, executed in steel wire in the 1950s. The open, linear construction draws volume in space, the shaped wires creating rhythm and transparency across the imposing format of H 150 × W 75 × D 34 cm. A refined example of mid-century Swedish sculptural craft, the work reads differently from every angle and pairs beautifully with both modern and classic interiors.

products.name: Sculpture by Nils G. Stenqvist
products.description: This sculptural work from the 1950s unfolds as a continuous, spiralling form. The compact, coiling movement evokes natural growth patterns, recalling shells, currents, and geological formations. The work is characteristic of Nils G. Stenqvist ’ s deep engagement with nature as both form and concept. Throughout his practice as a graphic artist, painter, and sculptor, Stenqvist repeatedly returned to organic structures, particularly the spiral, as a way of linking microcosmic phenomena such as cellular growth with larger cosmic and geological forces. His sculptures often explore this threshold between the intimate and the monumental, using simplified forms to suggest complex natural processes. Stenqvist was a central figure in Swedish modern art and is represented in major public collections, including Moderna Museet in Stockholm and museums in Gothenburg, Malmö, Kalmar, Hamburg, and the United States. Stamped.

products.name: Sculpture by Torsten Johansson
products.description: This lacquered iron sculpture was created in the 1980s and belongs to the later abstract phase of Torsten Johannson's work, when industrial materials and constructed forms became central to his practice. The composition is built around a vertical axis, articulated by bold geometric elements and contrasting surfaces in red and black. The figure-like structure suggests a totemic presence, yet remains non-figurative, defined instead by balance, symmetry, and material tension. Alongside his sculptural practice, the artist was also an influential furniture designer for the Swedish manufacturer AB Formträ. He is particularly known for the iconic “Honeycomb” wine rack.

products.name: Sculpture by Torsten Johansson
products.description: This iron sculpture was designed by Torsten Johansson in Denmark during the 1960s and reflects his distinctive approach to structure and modular form. Composed of intersecting rectilinear elements arranged around a central vertical support, the work presents a carefully balanced construction in which mass, rhythm, and proportion are held in precise tension. The dark, patinated iron surface is punctuated by gold-toned details, creating a subtle contrast that draws attention to the internal geometry of the piece. The sculpture belongs to a post-war Scandinavian abstract tradition that favoured non-figurative expression rooted in material and construction. Alongside his sculptural work, Johansson was a prominent furniture designer for the Swedish manufacturer AB Formträ, most notably responsible for the celebrated “Honeycomb” wine rack.

products.name: Sculpture 'Salome' by Anders Jönsson
products.description: The bronze sculpture Salome by Swedish artist Anders Jönsson presents the biblical figure in a poised, almost meditative moment rather than in overt drama. Kneeling on one leg with the other extended behind, Salome holds the head of John the Baptist in a shallow dish, her body balanced between movement and stillness. The simplified, rhythmic modeling of the figure, together with the flowing drapery over her knee, reflects the sculptural language of Nordic classicism from the early 20th century. Jönsson’s handling of bronze, with its rich green-brown patina, gives the surface a tactile depth that enhances the solemn mood of the scene. The work is signed by the artist and bears the foundry mark of Otto Meyers Eftr., underscoring its quality of execution. This Salome is an evocative example of Swedish figurative sculpture, where mythic subject matter, refined proportions and timeless material come together in a quietly powerful work. Signed.

The natural warmth of the wood and the rhythmic interplay between the panels give the triptych a calm, architectural presence on the wall. A characterful piece of mid-century Finnish craft, equally at home in a collector's living room or a Scandinavian-inspired interior.

products.name: Wall sculpture by Jörgen Larsen
products.description: This wall-mounted sculpture by Danish artist Jörgen Larsen, created in the 1970s, reflects the sculptural language associated with Scandinavian Brutalism. Constructed in forged iron, the composition is formed from a network of geometric elements—circles, arcs and linear bars—arranged in a carefully balanced structure. . The work emphasises the material qualities of iron, a characteristic feature of Brutalist design. Rather than concealing the fabrication process, the sculpture highlights the raw surface, weight and structural character of the metal. During the 1970s, Scandinavian artists increasingly explored abstract wall sculptures intended to function as focal points within modern interiors. Larsen’s work reflects this period’s interest in constructivist principles, where simple geometric forms are organised to create rhythm and balance.
